# A01-S47: Correspondence

Correspondence extract. Omissions are marked […].

[…]

First of all, Ellegaard is a skilled lawyer who understands how to 
litigate. The book is thus written as an argument for and against 
"robots" in legislative work and legal advising. When the word 
"robots" is in quotes, it is because Ellegaard makes a clear distinction 
between automation and autonomy.

[…]

Actually, Ellegaard raises more questions than he answers about the 
essential premises. This makes the book a discussion of whether 
the global and regional legal system (and thereby democracy, business 
agreements, ethics etc.) should be based on “the law”. He deals with 
for example current ICT regulation and human rights, and quite 
early comes to a conclusion that “Law as a Service”  (read: databases in the 
cloud like Google and chatbots) will be the likely implementation. 
This then raises the question of _private versus public_ ownership – and 
opens the global perspective, including that law is de facto in 
English, and that other nations with other languages will be subjected to a 
likely privately owned high-tech “law service” on/via the internet (?).

[…]
